claims.text: Processing route governs hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys by controlling microstructural refinement.
Additive manufacturing imposes more rapid cooling than conventional casting.
Rapid cooling during additive manufacturing produces finer grains than conventional casting.
Additive manufacturing produces a more uniform dispersion of secondary phases than conventional casting.
Fine grains and uniformly dispersed secondary phases increase barriers to dislocation motion.
The enhanced barriers to dislocation motion increase hardness and yield strength.
The controlled comparison will use identically composed samples made by additive manufacturing and conventional casting, with identical post-processing heat treatment.
Slower cooling during casting produces coarser grains.
Slower cooling during casting produces a less favorable dispersion of strengthening phases.
The coarser and less favorably dispersed cast microstructure provides lower resistance to deformation.
Additively manufactured samples will have statistically higher hardness than cast samples.
Additively manufactured samples will have statistically higher yield strength than cast samples.
Higher hardness and yield strength in additively manufactured samples will coincide with finer average grain size and a more uniform secondary-phase distribution.
The hypothesis is limited to compositions that avoid extensive phase segregation and brittle intermetallic formation.
The hypothesis is limited to processing regimes in which residual stresses remain moderate.
Extreme processing conditions may activate additional mechanisms that alter mechanical outcomes.
The magnitude of hardness and strength improvement may vary with alloy system and processing parameters.
Microstructural anisotropy may affect the measured mechanical properties.
Failure to observe statistically higher hardness and yield strength in additively manufactured samples would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a significantly finer and more homogeneous microstructure in additively manufactured samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.
